newsitem.title: CHINA: China to support HK if needed - central bank chief.
newsitem.headline: China to support HK if needed - central bank chief.

text.p: China's central bank will help the Hong Kong Monetary Authority if needed after the British colony reverts to Chinese rule on July 1, People's Bank of China governor Dai Xianglong was quoted on Wednesday as saying.

"Even though there may be some fluctuations in Hong Kong's financial markets before and after Beijing resumes sovereignty over the British colony on July 1, we fully believe the Hong Kong Monetary Authority will have the ability to handle the situation," Dai said in a front-page article in the Financial News.
Maintaining the financial stability of Hong Kong was not only the need of Hong Kong and mainland China but was required by the rest of the Asia-Pacific region, he said.

China would provide assistance to the Hong Kong Monetary Authority if needed but this help would be in line with Hong Kong's financial regulations and the Basic Law, the territory's mini-constitution after Beijing resumes sovereignty at midnight on June 30.
Under the terms of China's resumption of sovereignty over Hong Kong after more than 150 years of British colonial rule, the booming territory will retain its capitalist system for 50 years.
"We firmly believe that international financial circles (including Asia-Pacific central banks) will also provide active support to the financial stability of Hong Kong," Dai said.

Addressing the relationship between Hong Kong and Shanghai, he said: "I believe that as China's national economic centre, Shanghai's financial status is improving but from the short-term perspective, or at least before the yuan becomes fully convertible, Shanghai will not become an international financial centre.
"Even less will it replace Hong Kong," he wrote.

Shanghai has been eager to position itself as an alternative financial centre to Hong Kong, racing to develop its markets, but is expected to take many years before it can match the sophistication and importance of Hong Kong's markets.
Dai assured Hong Kong that the central bank had no plans to interfere with the territory's monetary system.
With two independent monetary systems in Hong Kong and the mainland, the People's Bank of China and the Hong Kong Monetary Authority would maintain their relative independence, Dai said.
China's central bank would not replace the Hong Kong Monetary Authority and would not set up a branch in Hong Kong, Dai said.
"The central bank will continue to strengthen its good cooperation with the Hong Kong Monetary Authority," he said.
